title: ICE-EM Mathematics 8 — Chapter 10: Rates and ratios

topics.title: Solving problems using the unitary method

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught unitary method by finding a per-item or convenient-group quantity and scaling; the donut part also interprets a two-donut serving.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 3 kg of potatoes cost $\$3.60$, find the cost of 4 kg.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 kg}&=\$3.60\div3=\$1.20\\\text{Cost of 4 kg}&=\$1.20\times4=\$4.80\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If 5 pens cost $\$15$, find the cost of 6 pens.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 pen}&=\$15\div5=\$3\\\text{Cost of 6 pens}&=\$3\times6=\$18\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If 8 tennis balls cost $\$15$, find the cost of 20 tennis balls.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 4 tennis balls}&=\$15\div2=\$7.50\\\text{Cost of 20 tennis balls}&=\$7.50\times5=\$37.50\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: If 9 billiard balls weigh 1440 g, how much do 6 billiard balls weigh?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Mass of 3 billiard balls}&=1440\div3=480\text{ g}\\\text{Mass of 6 billiard balls}&=480\times2=960\text{ g}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: If the length of a row of 12 seats is 480 cm, how long will a row of 21 seats be?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Length of a row of 3 seats}&=480\div4=120\text{ cm}\\\text{Length of a row of 21 seats}&=120\times7=840\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: The donuts of a certain donut manufacturer contain 25 g of fat ‘per standard serve’. If one standard serve is 2 donuts, how much fat, in grams, is consumed by a person who eats 5 donuts?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Fat in 1 donut}&=25\div2=12.5\text{ g}\\\text{Fat in 5 donuts}&=12.5\times5=62.5\text{ g}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 scale both quantities together, first dividing to one item or a convenient common unit, then multiplying to the requested quantity.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Each part directly applies proportional scaling to cost, mass or length. Rate problems is the closest catalogue skill; percentages and ratio sharing are not assessed.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The Chapter 10, Exercise 10A answer region individually lists 1a $4.80, matching 3.60 ÷ 3 × 4; 1b $18, matching 15 ÷ 5 × 6; 1c $37.50, matching 15 ÷ 2 × 5; 1d 960 g, matching 1440 ÷ 3 × 2; 1e 840 cm, matching 480 ÷ 4 × 7; and 1f 62.5 g, matching 25 ÷ 2 × 5. All six independently derived results agree with the printed key.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct proportional scaling using a unit quantity or a convenient common unit.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse cost-to-quantity relationships using unitary scaling, with the shares part requiring rounding down because only whole shares can be purchased.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 10 bananas cost $\$4$, how many can I buy for $\$14$?

answer.worked:
$\$4$ buys 10 bananas.

$\$2$ buys $10\div2=5$ bananas.

$\$14$ buys $7\times5=35$ bananas.

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many shares can I buy for $\$5400$ if 1000 shares cost $\$14$?

answer.short:
385714 whole shares

Use the number of shares bought for $\$7$ and round down to a whole share.
answer.worked:
$\$14$ buys 1000 shares.

$\$7$ buys $1000\div2=500$ shares.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Shares for }\$5400&=\frac{5400}{7}\times500\\\text{Shares for }\$5400&=\frac{2700000}{7}\\\text{Shares for }\$5400&=385714\frac{2}{7}.\end{align*}$$

Therefore, $\$5400$ can buy 385714 whole shares.

children.label: c
children.prompt: At a sale, exercise books cost $\$8$ per dozen. How many can I buy for $\$22$?

answer.worked:
$\$8$ buys 12 exercise books.

$\$2$ buys $12\div4=3$ exercise books.

$\$22$ buys $11\times3=33$ exercise books.

children.label: d
children.prompt: A caterer must buy 4 lettuces to make sandwiches for 50 people. How many lettuces will he need to buy to feed 225 people?

answer.worked:
50 people need 4 lettuces.

25 people need $4\div2=2$ lettuces.

225 people need $9\times2=18$ lettuces.

children.label: e
children.prompt: The first two pages of a student’s essay contain 800 words. How many pages are needed if the essay is to meet the requirement of 5000 words? (Assume that each page contains the same number of words.)

answer.worked:
800 words fill 2 pages.

400 words fill 1 page.

5000 words fill $5000\div400=12.5$ pages.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–4 divide to a convenient unit, then multiply to the requested quantity; Example 3 reverses a cost-to-quantity relationship and Example 4 retains exact fractions until the final interpretation.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–c find quantities from costs, d scales a catering quantity, and e finds pages from words. All directly assess proportional unitary reasoning.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Compared Exercise 10A row 2 against the original question parts: a shows 35, matching 14 ÷ 4 × 10; b shows 4500, conflicting with 5400 ÷ 14 × 1000; c shows 33, matching 22 ÷ 8 × 12; d shows 18, matching 225 ÷ 50 × 4; e shows 12.5, matching 5000 ÷ (800 ÷ 2).
answerEvidence.conflict: Part 2b: teacher key 4500 contradicts the printed givens; authored result is 385714 whole shares.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find quantities from proportional costs or amounts, including a non-integral intermediate result and whole-item interpretation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply proportional scaling to maps, shadows and a recipe.

children.label: a
children.prompt: On a map, 4 cm represents 2 km. How far apart are two suburbs A and B if they are 15 cm apart on the map?

answer.worked:
1 cm on the map represents $2\div4=0.5$ km.

15 cm on the map represents $15\times0.5=7.5$ km.

children.label: b
children.prompt: On a map, 10 cm represents a distance of 50 km. What distance on the map would represent 60 km?

answer.worked:
1 km is represented by $10\div50=0.2$ cm.

60 km is represented by $60\times0.2=12$ cm.

children.label: c
children.prompt: At a certain time of day, a man 1.8 m tall casts a shadow 2 m long. What is the height of a person who casts a shadow of length 1.8 m?

answer.worked:
A shadow of 1 m corresponds to a height of $1.8\div2=0.9$ m.

A shadow of 1.8 m corresponds to a height of $1.8\times0.9=1.62$ m.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If a tree of height 12 m casts a shadow of length 16.8 m, how long a shadow will a tree of height 9 m cast?

answer.worked:
A tree of height 3 m casts a shadow of length $16.8\div4=4.2$ m.

A tree of height 9 m casts a shadow of length $3\times4.2=12.6$ m.

children.label: e
children.prompt: A chef’s favourite cake recipe uses 8 eggs and 500 g of flour. If he scales the recipe up to use a dozen eggs, how many grams of flour should he use?

answer.worked:
4 eggs require $500\div2=250$ g of flour.

12 eggs require $3\times250=750$ g of flour.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–3 divide corresponding quantities to a convenient unit, then multiply to the required quantity.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Each part scales corresponding quantities; parts a–b use map scales, c–d use proportional shadows, and e scales a recipe.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Exercise 10A row 3 visibly gives a 7.5 km, b 12 cm, c 1.62 m, d 12.6 m and e 750 g. These individually match the two map scales, two shadow proportions and recipe calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale a known percentage to another percentage; part c also requires finding the additional number.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 100% of a school’s population is 840, what is 75% of the population?

answer.worked:
25% of the population is $840\div4=210$.

75% of the population is $3\times210=630$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If 60% of an amount is $\$540$, what is 40% of the amount?

answer.worked:
20% of the amount is $\$540\div3=\$180$.

40% of the amount is $2\times\$180=\$360$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: I own 32 copies of the 4 cent postage stamp issued by Jaga Jaga Island in 1930, and this is 20% of the total number of these stamps in existence. How many more of these stamps must I buy in order to own 25% of the total?

answer.worked:
A further $25\%-20\%=5\%$ of the total is needed.

5% of the total is $32\div4=8$ stamps, so 8 more stamps must be bought.

teachingContext.methodNote: Use a convenient common unit as in Examples 2–3, dividing first and then multiplying.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The quantities being scaled are percentages; part c asks for the additional 5%, rather than the final holding.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Exercise 10A row 4 visibly gives a 630, b $360 and c 8. Independent calculations give 75% of 840 = 630, 40/60 of $540 = $360, and an additional 5/20 of 32 = 8 stamps.

classification.difficultyReason: Use unitary calculations with fractional unit costs and a volume conversion.

inlines.text: These problems may require some written calculations.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 2 kg of tomatoes cost $\$5$, how many kilograms of tomatoes can I buy for $\$8$?

answer.worked:
$\$1$ buys $2\div5=0.4$ kg of tomatoes.

$\$8$ buys $8\times0.4=3.2$ kg of tomatoes.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If a dozen apples costs $\$5$, how much do 17 apples cost? Give your answer to the nearest cent.

answer.worked:
1 apple costs $\dfrac{5}{12}$ dollars.

17 apples cost $\dfrac{17\times5}{12}=\dfrac{85}{12}$ dollars.

The cost is $\$7.08$ to the nearest cent.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If 350 g of tinned pineapple contains 210 g of fruit, how much fruit will 500 g contain?

answer.worked:
50 g of tinned pineapple contains $210\div7=30$ g of fruit.

500 g contains $10\times30=300$ g of fruit.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If 750 mL of soft drink contains 288 g of sugar, how much sugar will 1 litre contain?

answer.worked:
1 litre is 1000 mL.

250 mL contains $288\div3=96$ g of sugar.

1000 mL contains $4\times96=384$ g of sugar.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–3 use convenient units; Example 4 retains an exact fractional unit cost until final rounding.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–d apply the unitary method to purchases and composition. Part b follows the exact-cost-then-round sequence of Example 4.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Exercise 10A row 5 visibly gives a 3.2 kg, b $7.08, c 300 g and d 384 g. Each agrees with the corresponding tomato purchase, apple cost rounded to cents, pineapple fruit content and one-litre sugar calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose fractional units and scale amounts, time, workforce or mass.

inlines.text: These problems can be done choosing a ‘unit’ that is a fraction.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Three-fifths of an amount is $\$243$. Find two-fifths of the amount.

answer.worked:
One-fifth of the amount is $\$243\div3=\$81$.

Two-fifths of the amount is $2\times\$81=\$162$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A man can cut down 12 trees in three-quarters of an hour. How many trees can he cut down in half an hour, working at the same rate?

answer.worked:
In one-quarter of an hour, he cuts down $12\div3=4$ trees.

In half an hour, he cuts down $2\times4=8$ trees.

children.label: c
children.prompt: One-third of the class can plant 28 plants during one period. How many plants could half of the class plant in the same time?

answer.worked:
One-sixth of the class can plant $28\div2=14$ plants in one period.

Half of the class can plant $3\times14=42$ plants in the same time.

children.label: d
children.prompt: 100 g of crispbread contains 1.2 g of saturated fat. How much crispbread contains 3 g of saturated fat?

answer.worked:
50 g of crispbread contains $1.2\div2=0.6$ g of saturated fat.

$3\div0.6=5$, so 3 g of saturated fat is contained in $5\times50=250$ g of crispbread.

children.label: e
children.prompt: The label on a certain cat medicine states that 3.2 mL should be given for every kilogram of body weight. How much medicine should be given to a kitten weighing 2.5 kg?

answer.worked:
For 0.5 kg, the amount of medicine is $3.2\div2=1.6$ mL.

For 2.5 kg, the amount of medicine is $5\times1.6=8$ mL.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 2–3 choose a convenient common unit. The embedded hint extends this approach to fractional units.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–c use fifths, quarter-hours and sixths of a class; d–e choose convenient fractional amounts before multiplying.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: Exercise 10A row 6 visibly gives a $162, b 8, c 42, d 250 g and e 8 mL. These individually agree with fractional amount scaling, half-hour tree cutting, half-class planting, crispbread mass and kitten medicine volume.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare unequal package sizes by finding costs for a common quantity, including recognising equal value.

content.prompt: If you are shopping, which is the better buy?

children.label: a
children.prompt: 400 g of tinned peaches costing $\$6.40$, or 550 g costing $\$9.00$

answer.worked:
Compare the costs of 100 g.

For the 400 g tin:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{640}{400}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{640}{400}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=160\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
For the 550 g tin:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{900}{550}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{900}{550}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{1800}{11}\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
Since $160<\frac{1800}{11}$, the 400 g tin costing $\$6.40$ is the better buy.

children.label: b
children.prompt: 500 g of lychees costing $\$5.50$, or 300 g costing $\$3.40$

answer.worked:
Compare the costs of 100 g.

For the 500 g package:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{550}{500}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{550}{500}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=110\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
For the 300 g package:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{340}{300}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{340}{300}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{340}{3}\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
Since $110<\frac{340}{3}$, the 500 g package costing $\$5.50$ is the better buy.

children.label: c
children.prompt: 140 g of toothpaste costing $\$1.68$, or 180 g costing $\$2.16$

answer.worked:
Compare the costs of 100 g.

For the 140 g tube:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{168}{140}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{168}{140}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=120\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
For the 180 g tube:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 1 g}&=\frac{216}{180}\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=\frac{216}{180}\times100\text{ cents}\\\text{Cost of 100 g}&=120\text{ cents}.\end{align*}$$
Both cost $\$1.20$ per 100 g, so they are the same value.

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–4 find a unit quantity by division and then multiply to obtain the required quantity; Example 4 retains exact fractions until rounding is requested.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Question 7 applies the taught unitary method to compare prices for equal masses. Best buys is the directly assessed skill.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The supplied teacher image lists Exercise 10A question 7a as 400 g, matching the cheaper peaches at 160 cents per 100 g; 7b as 500 g, matching the cheaper lychees at 110 cents per 100 g; and 7c as 'They are the same', matching both toothpaste tubes at 120 cents per 100 g. Each result was independently calculated from the corresponding student-page masses and prices.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale a packet price to a common mass, then compare prices and calculate the saving.

content.prompt: If a box of cereal is selling on special at $\$3.60$ for a 375 g packet, how much is 500 g of the cereal at this price? If there is actually a 500 g box selling for $\$4.50$, which is the cheaper way to buy 500 g of cereal, and by how much?

answer.short: $\$4.80$; the 500 g box is cheaper by 30 cents.
answer.worked:
Choose 125 g as the unit, since it is the highest common factor of 375 g and 500 g.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of 125 g}&=\$3.60\div3\\\text{Cost of 125 g}&=\$1.20\\\text{Cost of 500 g}&=\$1.20\times4\\\text{Cost of 500 g}&=\$4.80\\\text{Saving}&=\$4.80-\$4.50\\\text{Saving}&=\$0.30\end{align*}$$

The 500 g box selling for $\$4.50$ is cheaper by 30 cents.

teachingContext.methodNote: Example 2 chooses a common-factor unit, divides to find its cost, then multiplies to find the required quantity. Examples 1 and 4 also demonstrate proportional cost calculations.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Use 125 g as the common-factor unit to price 500 g, then compare equal masses. The directly assessed final skill is determining the best buy.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image lists Exercise 10A question 8 as $4.80, with the 500 g box cheaper by 30c. Independently scaling the source's $3.60 for 375 g gives $1.20 for 125 g and $4.80 for 500 g; comparison with the stated $4.50 box gives a $0.30 saving.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the time for one journey part, then scale to the four remaining parts.

content.prompt: A ship has taken 15 days to travel $\frac{3}{7}$ of its journey. How much longer will it take to complete the journey?

answer.worked:
Assuming the ship continues at the same rate:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Time for }\frac{1}{7}\text{ of the journey}&=15\div3=5\text{ days}\\\text{Remaining fraction}&=1-\frac{3}{7}=\frac{4}{7}\\\text{Time remaining}&=4\times5=20\text{ days}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–3 divide a known quantity into a convenient unit and multiply to obtain the required quantity. Here one seventh of the journey is the convenient unit.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The question applies the taught divide-then-multiply method to three known journey parts and four remaining parts; unitary-method-ratios is the closest supplied skill.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The student image shows Exercise 10A question 9: 15 days for three sevenths of a ship's journey, asking how much longer. The teacher image lists question 9 under Exercise 10A as ‘A further 20 days’. Independently, one seventh takes 15 ÷ 3 = 5 days and the remaining four sevenths take 4 × 5 = 20 days.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the time for one journey part, then scale to the four remaining parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate rooms, painters and time, recognising that more rooms increase time while more painters decrease it, then scale through painter-hours.

content.prompt: If 2 painters can paint 3 rooms in 9 hours, how long does it take for 3 painters to paint 4 rooms, working at the same rate?

answer.worked:
One painter takes twice as long as two painters to complete the same work.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Time for 1 painter to paint 3 rooms}&=2\times9=18\text{ hours}\\\text{Time for 1 painter to paint 1 room}&=18\div3=6\text{ hours}\\\text{Time for 1 painter to paint 4 rooms}&=6\times4=24\text{ hours}\\\text{Time for 3 painters to paint 4 rooms}&=24\div3=8\text{ hours}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–4 reduce a quantity to a convenient unit and then scale to the required quantity. The authored solution applies this sequence to one painter and one room before scaling to four rooms and three painters.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The task coordinates worker count, output and time, so related-rates-problems is the closest supplied catalogue skill. The inspected examples establish unitary scaling but do not explicitly demonstrate inverse worker/time scaling.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The supplied teacher image lists Exercise 10A question 10 as '8 hours'. The student image identifies question 10 by its 2 painters, 3 rooms and 9 hours givens and its request for 3 painters to paint 4 rooms. Independent unitary calculation gives 6 painter-hours per room and 24 painter-hours for four rooms, hence 8 hours with three painters.

localDifficulty.difficultyReason: Coordinate the number of painters, rooms and hours by reducing the work to one painter and one room.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the discounted price as 80% of the original and scale back to 100%, following the taught reverse-percentage method.

children.label: a
children.prompt: The price of a dress has been discounted by $20\%$ and the discounted price is $\$96$. What was the original price?

answer.worked:
The discounted price represents $100\%-20\%=80\%$ of the original price.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Value of }80\%&=\$96\\\text{Value of }20\%&=\$96\div4=\$24\\\text{Value of }100\%&=\$24\times5=\$120\end{align*}$$

The original price was $\$120$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Water is flowing out of a dam at a constant rate of 200 litres per hour. How much water has flowed out of the dam in 3 hours?

answer.worked:
In 1 hour, 200 litres flows out.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Water flowing out in 3 hours}&=200\times3\text{ litres}\\\text{Water flowing out in 3 hours}&=600\text{ litres}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If $10\%$ of a mine’s production in a day is 2100 tonnes, what is the total production for the day?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Production represented by }10\%&=2100\text{ tonnes}\\\text{Production represented by }100\%&=2100\times10\text{ tonnes}\\\text{Production represented by }100\%&=21\,000\text{ tonnes}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: If $70\%$ of an amount is $\$847$, what is the whole amount?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Value of }70\%&=\$847\\\text{Value of }10\%&=\$847\div7=\$121\\\text{Value of }100\%&=\$121\times10=\$1210\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: A car travels 96 km on 12 L of petrol. How much petrol would it use in travelling 200 km?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Petrol used for 1 km}&=\frac{12}{96}\text{ L}\\\text{Petrol used for 1 km}&=\frac18\text{ L}\\\text{Petrol used for 200 km}&=200\times\frac18\text{ L}\\\text{Petrol used for 200 km}&=25\text{ L}\end{align*}$$

Part c scales 10% to 100%; part d scales 70% to 10% to 100%. Part e finds litres per kilometre before scaling to 200 km. classification.difficultyReason: Each part uses a constant rate and a direct unitary calculation.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A car travelling at a constant speed travels 130 km in 2 hours. How far will it travel in 3 hours?

answer.worked:
In 1 hour, the car travels $130\div2=65$ km.

In 3 hours, the car travels $65\times3=195$ km.

children.label: b
children.prompt: A truck travels 55 km on 10 L of petrol. How far will it travel on 36 L?

answer.worked:
On 1 L, the truck travels $55\div10=5.5$ km.

On 36 L, the truck travels $5.5\times36=198$ km.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If 100 US dollars ($\text{US}\$100$) is worth 180 Australian dollars ($\text{A}\$180$), how much is $\text{US}\$40$ worth in Australian dollars?

answer.worked:
$\text{US}\$1$ is worth $\text{A}\$(180\div100)=\text{A}\$1.80$.

$\text{US}\$40$ is worth $\text{A}\$(1.80\times40)=\text{A}\$72$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: A watch loses 3 minutes every 6 months. How much time will it lose in 8 months?

answer.worked:
In 1 month, the watch loses $3\div6=\frac12$ minute.

In 8 months, the watch loses $\frac12\times8=4$ minutes.

children.label: e
children.prompt: A car travels 80 km on 12 L of petrol. How far could it travel on 300 L of petrol?

answer.worked:
On 1 L, the car travels $\frac{80}{12}=\frac{20}{3}$ km.

On 300 L, the car travels $\frac{20}{3}\times300=2000$ km.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover whole quantities from given percentages, identify the surviving percentage, and calculate a remaining quantity with rounding.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 20% of a farmer’s crop is 620 tonnes, what is the total crop?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Crop for }1\%&=620\div20=31\text{ tonnes}\\\text{Crop for }100\%&=31\times100=3100\text{ tonnes}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Nina is in hospital and has drunk 840 mL of water, which is 70% of her daily allowance. What is her daily allowance?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Water for }1\%&=840\div70=12\text{ mL}\\\text{Water for }100\%&=12\times100=1200\text{ mL}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If 120% of an amount is $\$156$, what was the original amount?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Amount for }1\%&=\$156\div120=\$1.30\\\text{Amount for }100\%&=\$1.30\times100=\$130\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hail destroyed 58% of a crop of plums, and only 10 500 kg was sent to market. How much would have been sent to market if there had been no hailstorm?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage remaining}&=100\%-58\%=42\%\\\text{Mass for }1\%&=10\,500\div42=250\text{ kg}\\\text{Mass for }100\%&=250\times100=25\,000\text{ kg}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: A farmer has used 6000 L of petrol harvesting his crop, and has so far harvested 35%. How much more petrol, correct to the nearest 100 L, will he need to harvest the whole crop?

answer.short:
$11\,100\text{ L}$ more.

The remaining 65% requires $\frac{65}{35}$ times the petrol already used.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage remaining}&=100\%-35\%=65\%\\\text{Petrol for }1\%&=6000\div35=\frac{1200}{7}\text{ L}\\\text{Petrol for }65\%&=\frac{1200}{7}\times65\\\text{Petrol for }65\%&=\frac{78\,000}{7}\text{ L}\\\text{Petrol for }65\%&\approx11\,100\text{ L}\end{align*}$$
The farmer needs 11 100 L more petrol, correct to the nearest 100 L.

Unitary-method-percentages covers the complete task, with reverse-percentage-problems supporting c and d.

The teacher image under Exercise 10B question 3 lists a 3100 t, b 1200 mL, c $130, d 25 000 kg, and e 11 100 L. classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate quantity-per-unit relationship and link unit-rate calculations with conversions such as hours to minutes or days to weeks.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A guesthouse has used 630 L of milk over a 30-day period. At what rate, in litres per week, is it using milk?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Milk used per day}&=630\div30\\\text{Milk used per day}&=21\text{ L/day}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Milk used per week}&=21\times7\\\text{Milk used per week}&=147\text{ L/week}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A firm pays its workers $\$1800$ per 40-hour week. What rate of pay is this in dollars per minute?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Pay per hour}&=1800\div40\\\text{Pay per hour}&=\$45/\text{h}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Pay per minute}&=45\div60\\\text{Pay per minute}&=\$0.75/\text{min}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: 350 megalitres of water has flowed into a dam in two and a half days. What is the average flow rate, in megalitres per day?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Water flowing per day}&=350\div2.5\\\text{Water flowing per day}&=140\text{ ML/day}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: A car has travelled 240 km on 48 L of petrol. At what rate, in litres per 100 km, is the car using petrol?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Petrol used per kilometre}&=48\div240\\\text{Petrol used per kilometre}&=\frac15\text{ L/km}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Petrol used per }100\text{ km}&=\frac15\times100\\\text{Petrol used per }100\text{ km}&=20\text{ L}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: A log of wood weighs 3 kg and has a volume of $2400\text{ cm}^3$. What is its density, in kilograms per $\text{cm}^3$?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Mass per cubic centimetre}&=\frac{3}{2400}\\\text{Mass per cubic centimetre}&=\frac{1}{800}\text{ kg/cm}^3\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: A woman has been paid $\$3800$ for 250 hours of work. At what weekly rate is she being paid, assuming there are 40 hours in a normal working week?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Pay per hour}&=3800\div250\\\text{Pay per hour}&=\$15.20/\text{h}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Pay per week}&=15.20\times40\\\text{Pay per week}&=\$608/\text{week}\end{align*}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: A battered old truck has driven the 740 km from Wagga Wagga to Wee Waa in $18\frac12$ hours. What was its average speed, in kilometres per hour?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Distance travelled per hour}&=740\div18.5\\\text{Distance travelled per hour}&=40\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

Page 7, Changing units and Example 8, demonstrates successive one-step rate conversions. Each solution first finds a quantity per one unit, then scales to the requested unit where necessary.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a, b, d and f convert practical rates through a unit rate; c and e simplify quantity-per-unit rates; g finds distance per hour. Rate problems is the closest whole-question skill, supported by rate-unit conversion, simplified rates and speed calculation.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A large tank is leaking water at 20 mL per second. Express this rate in litres per hour.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Leak rate}&=\frac{20}{1000}\text{ L/s}\\\text{Leak rate}&=0.02\times60\text{ L/min}\\\text{Leak rate}&=1.2\times60\text{ L/h}\\\text{Leak rate}&=72\text{ L/h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Every student in a school of 800 throws away an average of 200 g of rubbish a day. If there are 200 days in the school year, what is the rate at which the students throw away rubbish, in kilograms per year?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{School's daily rubbish}&=800\times200\text{ g/day}\\\text{School's daily rubbish}&=160\,000\text{ g/day}\\\text{School's daily rubbish}&=160\text{ kg/day}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{School's yearly rubbish}&=160\times200\text{ kg/year}\\\text{School's yearly rubbish}&=32\,000\text{ kg/year}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: The water stored in Warragamba Dam went from 41.6% of the dam’s capacity to 40.4% in a 30-day period. At what weekly rate, as a percentage of the dam’s total capacity, is the water being used?

answer.short: 0.28% of the dam’s total capacity per week.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Capacity used in 30 days}&=(41.6-40.4)\%\\\text{Capacity used in 30 days}&=1.2\%\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Daily use}&=\frac{1.2}{30}\%\\\text{Daily use}&=0.04\%\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Weekly use}&=7\times0.04\%\\\text{Weekly use}&=0.28\%\end{align*}$$
The stored water decreases by 0.28 percentage points of total capacity per week.

children.label: d
children.prompt: A car travels 100 km on 15 L of petrol. At what rate is the car using petrol, in units of kilometres per litre?

answer.worked:
15 L allows the car to travel 100 km.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Distance per litre}&=\frac{100}{15}\text{ km/L}\\\text{Distance per litre}&=\frac{20}{3}\text{ km/L}\\\text{Distance per litre}&=6\frac{2}{3}\text{ km/L}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: At a certain time, one Australian dollar bought 72 US cents.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Express $\text{A}\$12$ in US dollars.

answer.worked:
$\text{A}\$1$ buys $\text{US}\$0.72$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{US-dollar value of A}\$12&=12\times\$0.72\\\text{US-dollar value of A}\$12&=\$8.64\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Express $\text{US}\$18$ in Australian dollars.

answer.worked:
72 US cents buys $\text{A}\$1$, so 1 US cent buys $\text{A}\$\frac{1}{72}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Australian-dollar value of US}\$18&=\frac{1800}{72}\text{ Australian dollars}\\\text{Australian-dollar value of US}\$18&=\text{A}\$25\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: At a certain time, one Australian dollar bought 40 British pence. Express in Australian dollars the price of a jug that cost 55 British pounds. (There are 100 British pence in a British pound.)

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Jug price in British pence}&=55\times100\\\text{Jug price in British pence}&=5500\end{align*}$$
40 British pence buys $\text{A}\$1$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Jug price in Australian dollars}&=5500\div40\\\text{Jug price in Australian dollars}&=137.50\end{align*}$$
The jug costs $\text{A}\$137.50$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A truck has driven the 1050 km from Adelaide to Innamincka in $13\frac{1}{2}$ hours. What was its average speed, in kilometres per hour? Give your answer correct to the nearest kilometre per hour.

answer.worked:
In $13\frac{1}{2}$ hours, the truck travels 1050 km. Find the distance travelled per hour.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Average speed}&=1050\div\frac{27}{2}\\\text{Average speed}&=\frac{700}{9}\text{ km/h}\\\text{Average speed}&\approx78\text{ km/h}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A bullet is fired at a speed of 800 metres per second. What is its speed in kilometres per hour?

answer.worked:
Convert seconds to minutes, minutes to hours, then metres to kilometres.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Speed}&=800\text{ m/s}\\\text{Speed}&=800\times60\text{ m/min}\\\text{Speed}&=48\,000\times60\text{ m/h}\\\text{Speed}&=2\,880\,000\div1000\text{ km/h}\\\text{Speed}&=2880\text{ km/h}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: At a certain time, one Australian dollar bought 72 US cents.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Express $\text{A}\$21.06$ in US dollars, correct to the nearest US cent.

answer.worked:
$\text{A}\$1$ buys $\text{US}\$0.72$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{US dollar amount}&=21.06\times0.72\\\text{US dollar amount}&=15.1632\\\text{US dollar amount}&\approx15.16.\end{align*}$$

Therefore, $\text{A}\$21.06$ buys $\text{US}\$15.16$, to the nearest US cent.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Express $\text{US}\$21$ in Australian dollars, correct to the nearest Australian cent.

answer.worked:
$\text{US}\$0.72$ is worth $\text{A}\$1$, so $\text{US}\$1$ is worth $\text{A}\$\frac{1}{0.72}$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Australian dollar amount}&=21\div0.72\\\text{Australian dollar amount}&=\frac{175}{6}\\\text{Australian dollar amount}&\approx29.17.\end{align*}$$

Therefore, $\text{US}\$21$ is worth $\text{A}\$29.17$, to the nearest Australian cent.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If 20% of the marbles in a box are blue and there are 34 blue marbles, how many marbles are there in the box?

answer.worked:
20% represents 34 marbles.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Marbles represented by }10\% &=34\div2\\&=17\\\text{Marbles represented by }100\% &=17\times10\\&=170\end{align*}$$

There are 170 marbles in the box.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If 110% of an amount is $\$220$, what was the original amount?

answer.worked:
110% represents $\$220$.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Amount represented by }10\% &=\$220\div11\\&=\$20\\\text{Amount represented by }100\% &=\$20\times10\\&=\$200\end{align*}$$

The original amount was $\$200$.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the taught combined-work method to express both painters' outputs over a common interval, add outputs and convert back to time for one house.

content.prompt: Natalie can paint one house in 4 days, and Erin can paint one house in 5 days. Working at these rates, how long does it take if they work together?

inlines.text: In 20 days they paint 9 houses together, so one house takes 20 ÷ 9 days.

answer.worked:
Natalie paints 1 house in 4 days, so she paints 5 houses in 20 days.

Erin paints 1 house in 5 days, so she paints 4 houses in 20 days.

Together they paint $5+4=9$ houses in 20 days.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Time for one house}&=20\div9\text{ days}\\\text{Time for one house}&=\frac{20}{9}\text{ days}\\\text{Time for one house}&=2\frac{2}{9}\text{ days}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A plane is flying at a speed of 640 km/h. How far will it travel between 10:30 a.m. and 11:15 a.m. the same day?

answer.worked:
The elapsed time from 10:30 a.m. to 11:15 a.m. is 45 minutes.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Time}&=\frac{45}{60}\text{ h}\\\text{Time}&=\frac34\text{ h}\\\text{Distance}&=640\times\frac34\\\text{Distance}&=480\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Apply distance = speed × time after expressing the elapsed time in hours, following Example 11 and the unit-consistency warning.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Elapsed time is an intermediate step in a distance calculation.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher's 480 km matches a plane travelling at 640 km/h for the 45-minute interval from 10:30 a.m. to 11:15 a.m.

content.prompt: Henry travels 48 km by train in $\frac34$ of an hour and then cycles 12 km in $\frac12$ of an hour.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How long is he travelling in total?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Total time}&=\frac34+\frac12\\\text{Total time}&=\frac54\\\text{Total time}&=1\frac14\text{ h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is his average speed during the train trip?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Train speed}&=48\div\frac34\\\text{Train speed}&=48\times\frac43\\\text{Train speed}&=64\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is his average speed during the bike trip?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Bike speed}&=12\div\frac12\\\text{Bike speed}&=12\times2\\\text{Bike speed}&=24\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: What is his average speed over the whole trip?

answer.short:
$48\text{ km/h}$

Divide the total distance by the total time.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Total distance}&=48+12\\\text{Total distance}&=60\text{ km}\\\text{Average speed}&=60\div\frac54\\\text{Average speed}&=60\times\frac45\\\text{Average speed}&=48\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: The average-speed definition uses distance travelled divided by time taken. Apply it separately to stages and to the complete journey, retaining exact fractional hours as in Example 10.

answer.short:
$28\frac{1}{11}\text{ km/h}$

Divide the total distance by the total time in hours.
answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Total distance}&=\frac{1500}{1000}+40+10\\\text{Total distance}&=51.5\text{ km}\\\text{Total time}&=20+55+35\\\text{Total time}&=110\text{ min}\\\text{Total time}&=\frac{110}{60}\text{ h}\\\text{Total time}&=\frac{11}{6}\text{ h}\\\text{Average speed}&=51.5\div\frac{11}{6}\\\text{Average speed}&=\frac{309}{11}\text{ km/h}\\\text{Average speed}&=28\frac{1}{11}\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the last 15 laps?

content.prompt: Eliminate any fractions in these ratios, then reduce them to simplest form.

answer.worked:
Multiply both terms by $2$.

$$\begin{align*}2\frac{1}{2}:7&=(2\tfrac{1}{2}\times2):(7\times2)\\2\frac{1}{2}:7&=5:14\end{align*}$$

Multiply both terms by $3$, then divide by $2$.

$$\begin{align*}3\frac{1}{3}:8&=(3\tfrac{1}{3}\times3):(8\times3)\\3\frac{1}{3}:8&=10:24\\3\frac{1}{3}:8&=5:12\end{align*}$$

Multiply both terms by $10$, then divide by $5$.

$$\begin{align*}2.5:4.5&=25:45\\2.5:4.5&=5:9\end{align*}$$

The lowest common denominator is $20$; multiply both terms by $20$.

$$\begin{align*}6\frac{1}{5}:4\frac{1}{4}&=\frac{31}{5}:\frac{17}{4}\\6\frac{1}{5}:4\frac{1}{4}&=(\tfrac{31}{5}\times20):(\tfrac{17}{4}\times20)\\6\frac{1}{5}:4\frac{1}{4}&=124:85\end{align*}$$

Multiply both terms by the lowest common denominator, $8$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{3}{4}:\frac{5}{8}&=(\tfrac{3}{4}\times8):(\tfrac{5}{8}\times8)\\\frac{3}{4}:\frac{5}{8}&=6:5\end{align*}$$

Multiply both terms by the lowest common denominator, $9$.

content.prompt: In the diagram opposite, $ABCD$ is a square with diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meeting at $X$, $Z$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $Y$ is the midpoint of $XC$. Find the following ratios of areas.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 20, square diagram to the right
spec.description: Unshaded square with both diagonals and segments XZ and YZ. Ordinary source blue strokes become house black. Labels preserve their source sides.
spec.mathematics: A top left, B top right, C bottom right, D bottom left; X is the diagonal intersection; Z is the midpoint of BC; Y is the midpoint of XC.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry and labels are permanent givens; no answers are shown.

children.label: a
children.prompt: $\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXB)$

answer.worked: The diagonals divide the square into four equal-area triangles. Hence $\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD)=\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXB)$, so the ratio is $1:1$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZXB)$

answer.short:
$2:1$

The midpoint $Z$ halves the area of triangle $XBC$.
answer.worked:
Triangles $ZXB$ and $ZXC$ have equal bases $BZ=ZC$ and the same perpendicular height from $X$ to $BC$. Each has half the area of triangle $XBC$. Triangle $AXD$ has the same area as triangle $XBC$.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZXB)&=1:\frac12\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZXB)&=2:1\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: $\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZYC)$

answer.short:
$4:1$

Two successive midpoint divisions halve the area twice.
answer.worked:
Since $Z$ is the midpoint of $BC$, triangle $ZXC$ has half the area of triangle $XBC$. Since $Y$ is the midpoint of $XC$, triangles $ZXY$ and $ZYC$ have equal bases and the same perpendicular height from $Z$ to $XC$. Thus triangle $ZYC$ has one-quarter the area of triangle $XBC$, which equals the area of triangle $AXD$.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZYC)&=1:\frac14\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle AXD):\operatorname{area}(\triangle ZYC)&=4:1\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: $\operatorname{area}(\triangle DBC):\operatorname{area}(\triangle XYZ)$

answer.short:
$8:1$

Triangle $DBC$ contains two quarter-square triangles; triangle $XYZ$ is one-quarter of a quarter-square triangle.
answer.worked:
Triangle $DBC$ consists of the equal-area triangles $DXC$ and $XBC$, so its area is twice that of triangle $XBC$. The midpoint $Z$ halves triangle $XBC$, and the midpoint $Y$ halves triangle $ZXC$. Thus triangle $XYZ$ has one-quarter the area of triangle $XBC$.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(\triangle DBC):\operatorname{area}(\triangle XYZ)&=2:\frac14\\\operatorname{area}(\triangle DBC):\operatorname{area}(\triangle XYZ)&=8:1\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Express each ratio in simplest form.

answer.worked:
Divide every term by the HCF, $3$.

$$\begin{align*}33:9:12&=(33\div3):(9\div3):(12\div3)\\33:9:12&=11:3:4\end{align*}$$

Divide every term by the HCF, $5$.

$$\begin{align*}100:65:35&=(100\div5):(65\div5):(35\div5)\\100:65:35&=20:13:7\end{align*}$$

Multiply every term by $4$, then divide by the HCF, $5$.

$$\begin{align*}2\tfrac12:5:1\tfrac14&=\tfrac52:5:\tfrac54\\2\tfrac12:5:1\tfrac14&=10:20:5\\2\tfrac12:5:1\tfrac14&=2:4:1\end{align*}$$

Multiply every term by the lowest common denominator, $12$.

$$\begin{align*}1\tfrac13:2\tfrac12:3\tfrac14&=\tfrac43:\tfrac52:\tfrac{13}{4}\\1\tfrac13:2\tfrac12:3\tfrac14&=16:30:39\end{align*}$$

The whole-number terms have HCF $1$.

Multiply every term by the lowest common denominator, $6$.

$$\begin{align*}7:4\tfrac12:\tfrac16&=7:\tfrac92:\tfrac16\\7:4\tfrac12:\tfrac16&=42:27:1\end{align*}$$

The whole-number terms have HCF $1$.

Multiply every term by the lowest common denominator, $4$.

$$\begin{align*}11\tfrac12:20\tfrac12:22\tfrac14&=\tfrac{23}{2}:\tfrac{41}{2}:\tfrac{89}{4}\\11\tfrac12:20\tfrac12:22\tfrac14&=46:82:89\end{align*}$$

The whole-number terms have HCF $1$.

Measure the length of the Mawson Long Room on the printed plan; call this measurement $d$ cm. Convert its actual length to the same unit: $20\text{ m}=2000\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Scale}&=d:2000\\\text{Scale}&=1:\frac{2000}{d}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute your measured value of $d$ to obtain the approximate numerical scale.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, find the lengths of the frontages to James Street and Victoria Street, correct to the nearest metre.

answer.short: James Street: approximately $28$ m; Victoria Street: approximately $32$ m.
answer.worked:
Using the scale from part a, multiply each measured frontage by the scale factor and convert to metres. Equivalently, compare each frontage with the $20$ m room length on the same plan:
$$\begin{align*}L_{\text{James}}&\approx\frac{383}{275}\times20\text{ m}\\L_{\text{James}}&\approx28\text{ m}\\L_{\text{Victoria}}&\approx\frac{438}{275}\times20\text{ m}\\L_{\text{Victoria}}&\approx32\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the dimensions of the meeting room, correct to the nearest metre, and hence calculate its area, correct to the nearest square metre.

answer.short: Approximately $6\text{ m}\times6\text{ m}$; area approximately $36\text{ m}^2$.
answer.worked:
Compare the meeting-room sides with the $20$ m room length, or use the scale from part a:
$$\begin{align*}l&\approx\frac{83}{275}\times20\text{ m}\\l&\approx6\text{ m}\\w&\approx\frac{81}{275}\times20\text{ m}\\w&\approx6\text{ m}\\A&\approx6\times6\text{ m}^2\\A&\approx36\text{ m}^2.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Draw a plan of your bedroom (looking down from above) showing the positions of any doors and windows, and all items of furniture.

children.label: a
children.prompt: First measure the dimensions of your room, and work out a suitable scale that will allow you to draw the plan on a page of your exercise book.

answer.short: Answers vary. Sample: a $4\text{ m}\times3\text{ m}$ room at scale $1:50$ is drawn as $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
Sample room dimensions: $4\text{ m}\times3\text{ m}$. Choose scale $1:50$, so $1\text{ cm}$ represents $50\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Plan length}&=400\div50\\\text{Plan length}&=8\text{ cm}\\\text{Plan width}&=300\div50\\\text{Plan width}&=6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
An $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}$ plan fits on an exercise-book page.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Then measure the dimensions and position of each item in the room, reduce them to scale, and draw each item on the plan.

answer.short: Answers vary. Use the same scale for every item and its distance from the walls; include all doors, windows and furniture.
answer.worked:
Continue the sample using scale $1:50$. Convert each actual measurement to centimetres, then divide by $50$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bed length on plan}&=200\div50=4\text{ cm}\\\text{Bed width on plan}&=100\div50=2\text{ cm}\\\text{Desk length on plan}&=100\div50=2\text{ cm}\\\text{Desk depth on plan}&=50\div50=1\text{ cm}\\\text{Wardrobe length on plan}&=150\div50=3\text{ cm}\\\text{Wardrobe depth on plan}&=50\div50=1\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
In this sample, the bed touches the left and top walls. The desk touches the right wall and is $0.5\text{ m}$ from the top wall, so its top edge is $1\text{ cm}$ from that wall on the plan. The wardrobe touches the bottom wall and is $1\text{ m}$ from the right wall, so its right edge is $2\text{ cm}$ from that wall on the plan. The $1\text{ m}$ doorway and $1.5\text{ m}$ window become $2\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ respectively. Record the scale beside the completed plan.

children.prompt: Divide $735$ in the ratio $3:2$.

content.prompt: Reduce each ratio to simplest form:

answer.worked:
Divide both terms by their HCF, $3$.

$$6:3=2:1$$

Divide both terms by their HCF, $15$.

$$45:105=3:7$$

Divide both terms by their HCF, $16$.

$$16:96=1:6$$

Divide both terms by their HCF, $4$.

$$64:108=16:27$$

Divide all three terms by their HCF, $3$.

$$441:270:300=147:90:100$$

Divide all three terms by their HCF, $6$.

$$78:156:222=13:26:37$$

Convert to improper fractions, then multiply both terms by $4$.

$$\begin{align*}2\frac{1}{2}:3\frac{1}{4}&=\frac{5}{2}:\frac{13}{4}\\2\frac{1}{2}:3\frac{1}{4}&=10:13\end{align*}$$

Convert to improper fractions, multiply both terms by $8$, then divide both terms by $3$.

$$\begin{align*}1\frac{1}{2}:1\frac{1}{8}&=\frac{3}{2}:\frac{9}{8}\\1\frac{1}{2}:1\frac{1}{8}&=12:9\\1\frac{1}{2}:1\frac{1}{8}&=4:3\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Extract output per machinist per week, scale to the new workforce and divide the new production target by that output to find time.

content.prompt: A shirt manufacturer decides that he can supply 280 shirts in 4 weeks using 7 machinists. How long would it take for 15 machinists to produce 1000 shirts?

answer.short:
$6\frac{2}{3}$ weeks.

Find one machinist’s weekly output, then scale to 15 machinists.
answer.worked:
Assume each machinist works at the same constant rate.

Seven machinists produce 280 shirts in 4 weeks.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Weekly output of 7 machinists}&=280\div4=70\text{ shirts}\\\text{Weekly output of 1 machinist}&=70\div7=10\text{ shirts}\\\text{Weekly output of 15 machinists}&=10\times15=150\text{ shirts}\\\text{Time required}&=\frac{1000}{150}\text{ weeks}\\\text{Time required}&=\frac{20}{3}\text{ weeks}\\\text{Time required}&=6\frac{2}{3}\text{ weeks}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 1–4 reduce quantities to a convenient unit before scaling. Page 6 demonstrates output–time scaling and combining workers’ output in Example 7; page 7 demonstrates successive unit conversions. The solution first finds output per week, then per machinist, then scales the workforce.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Related rates is the closest catalogue match because output depends on both worker count and time. The inspected teaching supports the component unitary steps, but does not explicitly demonstrate this exact worker/output/time extension.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image’s left-column Review exercise entry 4 gives 6 2/3 weeks. The source question specifies 280 shirts, 4 weeks, 7 machinists, then 1000 shirts and 15 machinists. Independent calculation gives 280 ÷ 4 ÷ 7 = 10 shirts per machinist per week, 150 shirts per week for 15 machinists, and 1000 ÷ 150 = 6 2/3 weeks, agreeing with that entry.

content.prompt: Sally is knitting jumpers for newly born babies.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If she knits at a rate of 2 rows per minute, and each row of knitting contains 45 stitches, how many stitches per second does she knit?

answer.worked:
In 1 minute, Sally knits $2\times45=90$ stitches.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Stitches per second}&=\frac{90}{60}\\\text{Stitches per second}&=1\frac{1}{2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If it takes Sally 5 hours to knit a jumper, and there are 150 rows of knitting in each jumper, how many rows per minute does she knit?

answer.worked:
$5$ hours $=5\times60=300$ minutes.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Rows per minute}&=\frac{150}{300}\\\text{Rows per minute}&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If it takes Sally 4 hours to knit a jumper, and there are 144 rows of knitting in each jumper with, on average, 50 stitches per row, how many stitches per minute does she knit?

answer.worked:
$4$ hours $=4\times60=240$ minutes.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Rows per minute}&=\frac{144}{240}\\\text{Rows per minute}&=\frac{3}{5}.\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Stitches per minute}&=\frac{3}{5}\times50\\\text{Stitches per minute}&=30.\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a combines rows per minute with stitches per row, then divides by 60. Part b converts five hours to minutes before finding rows per minute. Part c finds rows per minute and scales by stitches per row. These are direct applications of the inspected unitary and successive-conversion methods.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate speed, distance or time relationship in each part and coordinate it with conversion between minutes and hours.

content.prompt: Joe walks every morning to keep fit.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If he walks a distance of $10$ km at an average speed of $6$ km/h, how long, in minutes, does his morning walk take him?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Time taken}&=\frac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{speed}}\\\text{Time taken}&=\frac{10}{6}\text{ h}\\\text{Time taken}&=\frac{5}{3}\times60\text{ min}\\\text{Time taken}&=100\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: If he walks a distance of $7$ km and it takes him $80$ minutes, what is his average speed, in km/h?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Time taken}&=\frac{80}{60}\text{ h}\\\text{Time taken}&=\frac{4}{3}\text{ h}\\\text{Average speed}&=\frac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time taken}}\\\text{Average speed}&=7\div\frac{4}{3}\text{ km/h}\\\text{Average speed}&=7\times\frac{3}{4}\text{ km/h}\\\text{Average speed}&=5\frac{1}{4}\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: If he walks at an average speed of $5$ km/h for $140$ minutes, how far does he walk?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Time taken}&=\frac{140}{60}\text{ h}\\\text{Time taken}&=\frac{7}{3}\text{ h}\\\text{Distance travelled}&=\text{speed}\times\text{time taken}\\\text{Distance travelled}&=5\times\frac{7}{3}\text{ km}\\\text{Distance travelled}&=11\frac{2}{3}\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Examples 9–10 calculate average speed by dividing distance by time, including fractional hours. Examples 11–13 and the Speed summary give distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed, with consistent units.
teachingContext.mappingNote: Part a uses the time formula and converts hours to minutes; part b converts minutes to hours before calculating average speed; part c converts minutes to hours before calculating distance. These directly assess calculate-speed-distance-time.

content.prompt: The total amount of prize money in a photography competition is $\$19\,600$. Given that the prize money is divided among the first, second and third prizes in the ratio $7:5:2$, find the amount each prize winner receives.

answer.worked:

content.prompt: A container is filled with 64 L of orange juice, then 12 L of juice are removed and the container is topped up with lemon juice. The juice is thoroughly mixed before 12 L of the mixture is removed and the container is again topped up with lemon juice. What is the ratio of orange juice to lemon juice in the final mixture?

answer.short:

The second removal takes away the same fraction of each juice as its fraction of the thoroughly mixed contents.
answer.worked:
After the first removal and refill, there are $64-12=52$ L of orange juice and $12$ L of lemon juice. Thorough mixing means that $\frac{52}{64}=\frac{13}{16}$ of the next amount removed is orange juice.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Orange juice removed next}&=12\times\frac{13}{16}\text{ L}\\\text{Orange juice removed next}&=\frac{39}{4}\text{ L}\\\text{Final orange juice}&=52-\frac{39}{4}\text{ L}\\\text{Final orange juice}&=\frac{169}{4}\text{ L}\\\text{Final lemon juice}&=64-\frac{169}{4}\text{ L}\\\text{Final lemon juice}&=\frac{87}{4}\text{ L}\\\text{Orange juice : lemon juice}&=\frac{169}{4}:\frac{87}{4}\\\text{Orange juice : lemon juice}&=169:87\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Two equal-sized vats, A and B, each containing 1000 L of oil, are being drained at a constant rate. It takes 4 hours to drain vat A completely and 5 hours to drain vat B completely. Find the time at which the amount of oil in vat B is four times the amount of oil in vat A.

inlines.text: 3.75 hours (3 hours 45 minutes) after draining begins.
Find each hourly drainage rate, then compare the volumes remaining.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{A's drainage rate}&=1000\div4=250\text{ L/h}\\\text{B's drainage rate}&=1000\div5=200\text{ L/h}\end{align*}$$
Compare four times the volume remaining in A with the volume remaining in B. Initially, the difference is
$$4\times1000-1000=3000\text{ L}.$$
Four times A's remaining volume decreases by $4\times250=1000$ L each hour, while B's remaining volume decreases by $200$ L each hour. Therefore, their difference decreases by $1000-200=800$ L each hour.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Time for the difference to reach zero}&=3000\div800\text{ h}\\&=3.75\text{ h}\end{align*}$$
At this time, A contains $1000-250\times3.75=62.5$ L and B contains $1000-200\times3.75=250$ L. Since $250=4\times62.5$, the required time is 3.75 hours, or 3 hours 45 minutes.

$$\begin{align*}\text{First concentrate volume}&=1\div6=\frac16\text{ L}\\\text{First water volume}&=5\times\frac16=\frac56\text{ L}\\\text{Second concentrate volume}&=\frac12\div5=\frac1{10}\text{ L}\\\text{Second water volume}&=4\times\frac1{10}=\frac25\text{ L}\\\text{Total concentrate volume}&=\frac16+\frac1{10}=\frac4{15}\text{ L}\\\text{Total water volume}&=\frac56+\frac25=\frac{37}{30}\text{ L}\\\text{Concentrate:water}&=\frac4{15}:\frac{37}{30}\\\text{Concentrate:water}&=8:37\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: A bottle contains one-third of a litre of cordial, which consists of water and cordial concentrate in the ratio $1:4$. Two-thirds of a litre of water are then poured in. What is the ratio of concentrate to water now?

answer.short:
$4:11$

The given ratio is water to concentrate; give the final ratio in the requested reverse order.
answer.worked:
The original cordial has $1+4=5$ parts.

$$\begin{align*}\text{One part}&=\frac13\div5=\frac1{15}\text{ L}\\\text{Concentrate volume}&=4\times\frac1{15}=\frac4{15}\text{ L}\\\text{Original water volume}&=\frac1{15}\text{ L}\\\text{Final water volume}&=\frac1{15}+\frac23=\frac{11}{15}\text{ L}\\\text{Concentrate:water}&=\frac4{15}:\frac{11}{15}\\\text{Concentrate:water}&=4:11\end{align*}$$

Paul travels at 60 kilometres per hour.

The Smith household uses 500 litres of water per day.

These are examples of rates. Rates are used here to measure speed and water consumption, and we encounter many different kinds of rates in everyday life. For example, Mary earns $15 an hour working at the supermarket.

entries.description: If the speed of an object does not change over time, we say that it is travelling with constant speed. For example, a car travelling at a constant speed of 60 kilometres per hour would travel 60 km in 1 hour. It would travel 120 km in 2 hours and 150 km in 2½ hours.

entries.description: Looking at things the other way around, if I travel at a constant speed for 100 km and it takes me 1 hour to complete the journey, then my speed is 100 kilometres per hour. entries.description: If the distance is measured in metres and the time is measured in seconds, the speed is measured in metres per second. If an athlete runs 100 metres in 10 seconds, her speed is 10 metres per second. This is usually written as 10 m/s.

entries.description: When we drive a car or ride a bike, it is very rare for our speed to remain the same for a long period of time. Most of the time, especially in the city, we are slowing down or speeding up, so our speed is not constant. If we travel 20 km in 1 hour, then we say that our average speed is 20 km/h, even though we may have travelled much faster than this at some times in that hour, and come to a complete stop at others. When we calculate speed, we often mean average speed, and in all our unitary method calculations in this chapter we make the assumption of constant speed.

average speed = distance travelled/time taken
= 6 ÷ 3/4
= 6/1 × 4/3
= 8

Alternatively, we can use unitary method to work out speeds.

Paul rides 6 km in 3/4 of an hour.
[÷ 3] Paul rides 2 km in 1/4 of an hour.
[× 4] Paul rides 8 km in 1 hour.

entries.description:
A scale drawing is used where an object being illustrated is too large to be shown at full size on the page. For example, a scale drawing might be used to show:
• the plan of a building
• a map of a suburb or a country
• a photograph of a distant galaxy.
Scale drawings are also used when very small objects are to be shown, such as:
• a diagram of a cross-section of skin or hair
• an enlargement of an image on a computer screen
• a magnified photograph of an insect.

entries.description:
A scale drawing has the same shape as the original object, but a different size. All the lengths of the original object are reduced or magnified in the drawing in exactly the same ratio. This ratio is called the scale of the drawing.
